strengths: Introduces a clear and interesting controlled formulation—Programming by Backprop—for testing whether models can use programs encountered only as source code to answer later input-specific questions.
The two temporal settings, Proactive-PBB and Retroactive-PBB, provide a useful experimental decomposition of the phenomenon.

Experiments span synthetic arithmetic programs, Leetcode tasks, and custom ciphers, as well as multiple Llama model sizes and GPT-4o; the arithmetic programs and custom ciphers help limit direct pretraining contamination.

The results contain several informative observations, including scaling trends, explicit versus implicit execution, limited program composition, code versus natural-language representations, and differences among SFT, DPO, and GRPO.
The paper is clearly motivated and generally well written, and it includes useful data-scaling, curriculum, representation, and optimization ablations.
weaknesses: The central conclusion is substantially overstated. The experiments show parametric retrieval and execution of particular short programs after controlled finetuning, but do not demonstrate improved general-purpose reasoning or establish that this mechanism explains the broader benefits of code pretraining.

All training experiments use a single seed. Moreover, the reported confidence intervals are computed over 16 sampled generations per problem and therefore do not capture training-run variability; treating correlated generations as the primary uncertainty source risks overly narrow intervals.

Several important comparisons are confounded. The cipher code condition receives Leetcode code/I-O training followed by cipher source code, whereas the I/O condition receives a different cipher demonstration distribution. Consequently, the claimed robustness advantage cannot be attributed cleanly to source code rather than curriculum, data volume, or training-distribution differences.

The Leetcode evidence is difficult to interpret because the authors explicitly expect these programs to occur in pretraining. The modest gain from stage 2 may reflect reminding or retrieval of memorized solutions rather than acquisition of new algorithmic abstractions.

The natural-language comparison is insufficient to establish that code syntax is intrinsically special: it uses only one description style, lacks controls for tokenization, length, formatting, and pretraining familiarity, and performance depends strongly on prompt/preamble augmentation.

Absolute performance on the contamination-resistant arithmetic setting is fairly low—approximately 30% at best and often much lower for direct or composed execution—so claims that models acquire reusable algorithmic abstractions should be qualified. Per-operation, per-program-family, and systematic out-of-distribution analyses are missing.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: the reward and answer-verification procedure, output parsing, DPO data construction and hyperparameters, several SFT settings, exact GPT-4o snapshot, and per-cipher results are not adequately specified. Reliance on a proprietary API model further limits verification.

The crucial MathInstruct mixture used during code-only stage 2 is described as necessary but is not adequately ablated. This makes the source-code-only characterization less clean and leaves open how much the result depends on maintaining or eliciting generic mathematical instruction-following behavior.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and potentially important question: whether models can internalize executable procedures from source code without seeing corresponding input-output examples.

The two-stage proactive and retroactive settings are conceptually clear, and the study covers synthetic arithmetic programs, Leetcode problems, custom ciphers, multiple model sizes, direct prediction, and chain-of-thought inference.
Several results are suggestive, including scaling with model size, the comparison between code and natural-language descriptions, limited composition experiments, and the SFT/DPO/GRPO comparison.
The manuscript is generally well written, candidly acknowledges pretraining contamination for Leetcode and the limitations of GPT-4o, and provides useful dataset-size and training-method ablations.
weaknesses: The central causal interpretation is not established because the proactive experiments lack the most important control: training on the code-only second stage, with the same MathInstruct mixture and training budget, but without the first-stage code-I/O curriculum. A pretrained code model may already know how to interpret code, while repeated code-only training merely associates each arbitrary function name with its definition. Without this control, improvements cannot confidently be attributed to the proposed transfer mechanism.

The random-arithmetic evaluation does not convincingly distinguish algorithm execution from shortcuts. Test inputs remain inside the same small finite range as the dataset, and the paper provides no analysis of output entropy, constant or low-variation functions, majority-output baselines, or accuracy on extrapolated inputs. Random combinations involving integer division, modulo, conditionals, and absolute value can generate many easy or degenerate functions. Consequently, the modest reported accuracy may not demonstrate reusable algorithmic abstractions.

The paper repeatedly makes claims stronger than its evidence, including that models 'develop reusable algorithmic abstractions,' that code training explains improvements in general-purpose reasoning, and that the GRPO result shows benefits from on-policy learning. The experiments demonstrate behavioral associations under a specialized finetuning protocol, not the internal mechanism claimed in the title; there is no representation analysis or decisive behavioral test of abstraction.

The cipher comparison is substantially confounded. Code training and I/O training differ in curriculum, data distribution, representation, and likely training exposure. There is no matched code-only control without Leetcode priming, no uniformly sampled I/O baseline, and no code-plus-I/O condition. Thus the experiment does not isolate why the code-trained model is more uniform across shifts.

The evidence is statistically weak for a top-tier claim. Every training experiment uses only one seed, while the reported confidence intervals are based on repeated stochastic generations and therefore do not capture variation due to training, program splits, or data generation. The apparent precision of the plots is consequently misleading.

The Leetcode experiments offer limited support because the authors acknowledge that the problems and solutions are likely present in model pretraining. The additional gain after exposing the model to source code may reflect retrieval or memorization rather than learning a new procedure.

The comparison of SFT, DPO, and GRPO does not isolate on-policy learning: the methods differ in objectives, sample generation, negative examples, and potentially effective compute. Critical DPO construction details and matched-budget controls are absent.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The appendix gives only minimal optimizer settings and omits important details such as SFT batch sizes, sequence lengths, exact prompts and parsing rules, reward definitions, DPO hyperparameters and preference construction, checkpoint selection, and complete GPT-4o finetuning configurations. Overall, the idea is promising, but missing controls and overextended mechanistic claims place the submission below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper identifies a novel and conceptually interesting form of out-of-context generalization: models learn to evaluate named programs from source-code exposure without program-specific I/O demonstrations. The proactive/retroactive distinction provides a useful experimental framework.

The central phenomenon is demonstrated across random arithmetic programs, Leetcode tasks, and custom ciphers, with multiple Llama model sizes and GPT-4o. The custom programs and ciphers help reduce concerns that all results arise from direct pretraining memorization.

The evaluation includes meaningful ablations and extensions: direct versus chain-of-thought inference, code versus natural-language descriptions, model and dataset scaling, program composition, one- versus two-stage training, and SFT/DPO/GRPO comparisons.

Several findings are practically and scientifically valuable: performance scales with model size; explicit reasoning improves execution of longer programs; code is substantially more effective than the tested natural-language representation; and source-code training produces more uniform cipher performance across parameter values than biased I/O demonstrations.

The paper is clearly written, well motivated, visually polished, and appropriately connects the results to out-of-context reasoning, algorithm distillation, and the role of code in language-model training.
weaknesses: The broad claim that code training explains improved general-purpose reasoning is stronger than the evidence. The experiments establish a controlled finetuning phenomenon on relatively small synthetic procedures, but do not directly study large-scale pretraining or transfer to unrelated reasoning tasks.

All training experiments use a single seed. Confidence intervals over 16 sampled generations quantify decoding variation rather than variation across training runs, so they do not establish the robustness or statistical significance of comparisons between training methods.

Several important controls are missing or insufficiently isolated. These include code-only training without prior code-I/O priming on the main random-arithmetic setting, shuffled or semantically incorrect program definitions, matched-compute repetition/memorization controls, and stronger natural-language representations matched for formatting and pretraining familiarity.

The SFT, DPO, and GRPO comparison does not convincingly isolate the claimed advantages of negative or on-policy samples. The methods differ in generated samples, optimization trajectory, and likely effective compute; the appendix provides too little detail to verify that training budgets are comparable.

The Leetcode evidence is difficult to interpret because the authors acknowledge likely pretraining contamination, while the GPT-4o results rely on an opaque API model that may use undisclosed inference mechanisms. These experiments broaden the evidence but are weaker causal tests than the synthetic setting.

Reproducibility details are incomplete despite the stated intent to release datasets. The paper omits important information such as precise prompt templates and augmentation sets, batching and sequence-length details for SFT, reward and stopping specifications for GRPO, DPO data construction, evaluation parsing, and the exact GPT-4o model snapshot.

Absolute accuracy on the clean synthetic tasks remains modest—roughly 0.3 in the strongest reported random-arithmetic condition—and implicit composition is especially weak. This limits the current practical significance and calls for more analysis of failure modes.
The discussion of constitutional alignment is speculative and is not supported by behavioral or safety experiments in the paper.

strengths: Introduces a clear and practically interesting formulation of learning executable behavior from declarative training-time instructions, with proactive and retroactive curricula that are easy to understand and potentially useful.

The controlled separation between instructions with and without execution supervision provides convincing evidence that the complete curriculum transfers procedural information beyond directly demonstrated behaviors.
Evaluation spans synthetic arithmetic programs, Leetcode problems, custom ciphers, and context-free grammars, with broadly consistent trends across Qwen, Llama, and GPT-4o model families.

The stage ablations, instruction-representation comparison, model- and data-scaling studies, RL/SFT/DPO comparison, composition experiment, and single-stage baseline collectively provide substantial empirical coverage.

The sample-efficiency result is notable: after a shared meta-training stage, one declarative instruction can perform comparably to many task-specific execution demonstrations. The paper appropriately acknowledges that this excludes the amortized cost of the first stage.
The paper is clearly motivated and written, and it candidly reports important limitations such as imperfect execution fidelity and weaker results for natural-language specifications.
weaknesses: The central mechanism is not established as strongly as the terminology suggests. Outputting correct answers without visible chain-of-thought does not demonstrate that a model internally executes or tracks algorithmic state; behavioral approximation or learned shortcuts remain possible. No mechanistic analysis or sufficiently diagnostic tests distinguish these explanations.

The evaluation reports confidence intervals over sampled generations but does not establish robustness across independent training runs, dataset partitions, curriculum orders, or hyperparameter choices. Training stochasticity may be material, especially for the smaller effects.

The sample-efficiency comparison counts task-specific examples but is not a complete compute-, token-, or data-matched comparison. PBB relies on a costly first-stage meta-training curriculum, instructions are revisited over multiple epochs, and the homogeneous single-stage baseline nearly closes the gap when instruction repetitions increase.

Novelty is somewhat limited by the paper's own observation that proactive PBB closely mirrors the two-stage implicit meta-learning pipeline of Krasheninnikov et al. The main advance is a useful framing and broader empirical study rather than a fundamentally new optimization method or theoretical result.

Several evaluations admit alternative explanations. Leetcode has high zero-shot performance and only modest gains, making memorization or familiar-domain adaptation difficult to exclude. CFG validity alone does not measure diversity or coverage and may reward repeatedly generating a small set of short, broadly compatible strings.

Natural-language instructions—the most practically relevant setting—perform substantially worse than code, while the paper's claim that this is merely a scaling or representation issue is speculative.

The broad safety conclusion is under-supported: controlled, deliberately constructed finetuning curricula do not by themselves show that incidental instructions in ordinary pretraining data will induce unintended executable behaviors.

Reproducibility details are incomplete, including independent seed counts, exact evaluation-set sizes and aggregation procedures, optimizer and finetuning configuration, sequence lengths, dataset-generation specifications, and decoding/format-handling details. The manuscript's displayed repository location is also absent.

strengths: The paper studies an interesting and relevant question: whether declarative specifications encountered during training can influence execution behavior without being supplied at inference time.
The proactive and retroactive curricula are clearly motivated, and the stage-wise ablations provide useful evidence that ordering matters rather than mere exposure to the same broad data types.
Experiments cover multiple model sizes and two model families, with an additional GPT-4o study, and include both algorithmic execution and formal-grammar generation.
The paper acknowledges important limitations, including the amortized cost of proactive Stage 1, weak natural-language performance, and the gap between PBB and in-context execution.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the claimed mechanism. Because each evaluation instruction is trained in association with the same task identifier later used as a prompt, the model could memorize and internally retrieve the specification and then use its existing code-execution ability. The paper provides no retrieval, aliasing, identifier-remapping, shuffled-specification, or mechanistic controls that distinguish this explanation from genuinely compiling procedural behavior.

The assertion that direct answers demonstrate implicit multi-step execution within a forward pass is unsupported. Absence of visible chain-of-thought does not establish how the model computed the answer, and no analysis excludes shortcuts or hidden retrieval of the memorized program.

The headline claim that one instruction is worth 100 examples is too strong. It is demonstrated narrowly on one synthetic benchmark and model, is not normalized by tokens or training compute, and counts a specification seen over five epochs as a single instruction. The expensive meta-training stage is shared by both methods but still substantially limits the practical interpretation.

Dataset construction is underspecified in ways that affect validity: the input ranges and held-out-input protocol, semantic duplication among random functions, program-complexity distribution, CFG generation and depth parameters, Leetcode filtering and contamination controls, and exact task prompts are not adequately documented.

Uncertainty is based on 16 generated samples, apparently from the same trained checkpoint, rather than independent training seeds or dataset splits. Thus the reported confidence intervals do not capture optimization or split variance, and no significance tests support many of the comparisons.

Baselines are incomplete. The homogeneous-mixture comparison is relegated to a single Llama setting, while matched-compute curriculum controls, repeated-instruction baselines across primary models, alternative continual-learning schedules, and controls using irrelevant or corrupted specifications are absent.

External validity is limited: the strongest evidence comes from artificial arithmetic programs and grammars, natural-language specifications perform substantially worse, Leetcode starts with high zero-shot accuracy, and retroactive PBB offers little benefit there. This does not support broad claims of generalization or practical programmability.

The safety conclusion is speculative. Controlled memorization of explicitly trained synthetic specifications does not by itself show that incidental natural-language instructions in realistic pretraining corpora will induce unintended behaviors.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate: the manuscript's promised repository link is blank, several optimization and generation details are missing, GPT-4o is not independently reproducible, and the Figure 3 caption and surrounding text repeatedly swap the locations of the composition and retroactive-PBB panels.

strengths: The paper introduces a clear and potentially important problem: converting declarative specifications encountered during training into reusable behaviors encoded in model parameters.

The proactive and retroactive curricula are intuitive, well motivated, and supported by strong stage-wise ablations showing that instruction-only or execution-only training does not explain the main results.

The empirical scope is substantial: two model families at multiple scales, GPT-4o fine-tuning, SFT/RL/DPO comparisons, code and natural-language representations, compositional execution, scaling analyses, and a distinct context-free-grammar domain.

The comparison with algorithm distillation provides compelling evidence of sample efficiency after amortizing the initial meta-training stage. The biased-cipher experiment further demonstrates a useful complementarity between declarative specifications and demonstrations.
The paper reports limitations honestly, particularly the sizable reliability gap relative to in-context execution, and its findings are relevant to both training-data design and AI safety.
weaknesses: The headline claim that one instruction is worth 100 examples is demonstrated primarily on synthetic random arithmetic with one model/configuration. It means comparable—not consistently superior—accuracy, and excludes the potentially large amortized cost of Stage 1. Replication on Leetcode, grammars, additional models, and multiple training seeds would make this claim substantially stronger.

Reported confidence intervals appear to reflect repeated decoding samples rather than independent fine-tuning runs. Training-seed variance is therefore unquantified, which matters for multi-stage SFT and especially RL/DPO experiments.

The homogeneous single-stage-mixture baseline central to the curriculum claim is relegated to one Llama-8B experiment. Its comparison varies instruction repetitions, but token counts, optimizer steps, and total training compute do not appear rigorously matched. More compute-matched baselines across models and domains are needed.

The conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental relative to implicit meta-learning and out-of-context reasoning; proactive PBB is acknowledged to closely mirror an existing two-stage pipeline. The formalization largely redescribes standard gradient updates and does not explain why or when the proposed behavior should emerge.

Generalization remains narrow: train and evaluation procedures are sampled from the same synthetic generators, grammar splits are not shown to hold out structural families, and Leetcode may overlap semantically with pretraining. Stronger distribution shifts would better substantiate claims of acquiring general procedural knowledge.

Several mechanistic interpretations are stronger than the evidence. Correct outputs without visible chain-of-thought do not establish that all multi-step computation occurs internally, and behavior on synthetic tasks alone offers limited support for the broader safety conclusion about unintended real-world behaviors.

Reproducibility details are incomplete, including independent run counts, optimizer and sequence-length settings, exact dataset-generation/split procedures, checkpoint/API versions, evaluation prompting, and failure-handling rules. The promised repository link is absent from the supplied manuscript, so the resources cannot currently be assessed.
